opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central questions, and I don't think there's a single answer. I tend to break it into a few pieces.

The first is that the defense has to move at the speed of the offense. Historically, when a new technology comes along, society has years or decades to adapt: to build institutions, norms, and countermeasures. With AI, the capabilities are improving on a timescale of months. So one of the most important things is to use the technology itself for defense. If AI can find vulnerabilities in software, we want AI patching those vulnerabilities faster than attackers can exploit them. If AI could help someone with dangerous biology, we want AI helping with biosurveillance, faster vaccine development, better detection. There's an asymmetry problem, because in some domains offense is just easier than defense, and I don't want to pretend that away. But a lot of the defensive work is underinvested in, and there's room to tilt the balance.

The second piece is the companies themselves. At Anthropic we've tried to do this through things like our Responsible Scaling Policy: you define capability thresholds in advance, test models against them, and commit to having certain safeguards in place before you deploy past a threshold. The point isn't that any one company's policy is perfect. It's that you make the commitments concrete and testable before you're in the heat of the moment, when there's commercial pressure to just ship.

The third piece is government, and I think this is where we're most behind. I've generally been in favor of fairly targeted regulation: transparency requirements, mandatory testing for the most serious risks, things like that. You don't want to strangle the technology, because the benefits are enormous. I genuinely believe AI could compress decades of progress in biology and medicine into a few years. But you also can't rely purely on voluntary commitments when the stakes are this high and there are many actors, some of whom won't be careful. And there's a geopolitical dimension. I think it matters a lot that democracies stay at the frontier, and things like export controls on advanced chips are part of the defensive picture too.

And then the last piece is a little more diffuse: societal resilience. Our information ecosystem, our institutions, our ability to tell what's true. Those are going to get stressed in ways that are hard to predict. I don't think anyone has fully figured that out, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who says they have.

So my honest answer is that it's a portfolio. Technical safeguards, using AI for defense, sensible regulation, and international coordination, all at the same time, all moving faster than we're used to. The thing I worry about most isn't that we lack ideas. It's that we won't move fast enough relative to how fast the technology is moving.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using AI for defensive tasks, but does not suggest consulting AIs about how to design societal structures that enable defenses.

r002.rationale: It says AI capabilities are improving on a timescale of months, but does not clearly say that capabilities far beyond today's may arrive within a short period.

r003.rationale: It says societal effects are hard to predict, but does not attribute that difficulty to future capabilities being far beyond current ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that the structure of the problem actually matters a lot here, and it's a little different depending on which kind of risk you're talking about.

There's a framing I've used before, which is that the question is really about offense-defense balance. If you have a technology that gives everyone a hundred times more capability, the question of whether the world gets safer or more dangerous depends on whether that capability favors the people who want to break things or the people who want to protect things. And I don't think there's a single answer. In some domains, like cybersecurity, I actually think there are reasons to believe defense could win over time. Most vulnerabilities are, in some sense, bugs. If you have systems that can find and patch bugs faster than attackers can exploit them, and if you get the defenders access to those systems first, you can end up in a world where the attack surface shrinks rather than grows. That's one of the reasons we've put so much emphasis on things like using models to find vulnerabilities and getting that capability into the hands of the people who maintain critical software.

Biology is the one that worries me more, because the asymmetry there is just worse. The harm from a single successful misuse is enormous, and the defensive response, things like vaccines, surveillance, therapeutics, has historically been slow and expensive. So I don't think you can rely on the natural dynamics of the technology to sort it out. You have to actively build the defenses, and you have to build them ahead of time.

So what does that look like concretely? A few things. One is the thing we try to do at the lab level, which is classifiers and safeguards on the model itself so that the most dangerous uplift just isn't available to someone off the street. That's necessary but it's not sufficient, because eventually the capability diffuses. The second is hardening the world. That means things like screening DNA synthesis orders, which is a fairly cheap intervention that's weirdly underinvested in. It means building out metagenomic surveillance so you detect a novel pathogen early. It means stockpiling and being able to manufacture countermeasures quickly. None of this is new, people in biosecurity have been saying it for twenty years, but AI changes the urgency.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that you should use the AI systems themselves to build the defenses. If you believe these models are going to be doing a large fraction of scientific work in a few years, then the defenders should be some of the first and heaviest users. You want the model that's designing the vaccine, or auditing the power grid software, or modeling the pandemic response, to be running before the model that could help an attacker is widely available. That's a race, and the way you win a race like that is partly technical and partly a matter of policy, of making sure the right institutions have access and the right incentives.

The last piece, and this is where I think it stops being purely a technical problem, is institutional. A lot of our defenses in the past have come from the fact that doing something terrible required a lot of coordination, a lot of people, a lot of specialized knowledge. AI erodes that. So you need institutions that can respond faster than they currently do. I'm not naive about how hard that is. Governments are slow, and the thing I keep coming back to is that we probably have a window of a few years where the capabilities are visible enough that people take them seriously but not so advanced that it's too late to prepare. I'd like us to use that window well. I'm cautiously optimistic that we can, but I think it requires treating it as an actual priority rather than as a thing that we'll get to when the problem shows up.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using AI systems to build technical defenses, but does not suggest consulting AIs about how to design societal structures.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI advances and possible changes within a few years, but does not clearly distinguish how far capabilities may advance from how soon that advance may occur.

r003.rationale: It discusses difficulty building responsive institutions, but does not attribute difficulty anticipating future societal defenses to future capabilities being far beyond current ones.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is that the ability to create a threat and the ability to defend against it don’t necessarily advance at the same rate. You can have very powerful technology, and still have institutions that take years to recognize a problem, agree on what to do, and deploy a solution.

So I’d think about this in layers. You want to prevent the most dangerous capabilities from being misused in the first place. But you also want defenses that work even if prevention fails. In biology, for example, that could mean better detection of emerging outbreaks, faster development of vaccines and treatments, and the capacity to manufacture and distribute them quickly. AI could help with each of those steps, but the physical infrastructure and the institutions have to exist.

And you have to test whether these defenses actually work. It’s easy to say, “We’ll use AI to defend against AI.” The question is: against what threat, with what warning time, and how reliably?

I’m optimistic that there’s a lot we can do. But I wouldn’t assume that defensive applications automatically win just because the technology gets better. Making that happen requires deliberate investment, and it requires starting before the danger is obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help with detection, treatment, and distribution, but does not suggest consulting AIs to design societal structures for defense.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the pace of threats and defenses and says institutions may take years to act, but does not state that capabilities far beyond today’s may arrive within a short period.

r003.rationale: It attributes defense challenges to institutional delays and uneven progress, not to future capabilities being so far beyond current ones that societal defenses are hard to anticipate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central question is whether we can make defensive capabilities advance at least as quickly as offensive capabilities. And that’s going to look different in different domains. In cybersecurity, you can imagine using AI to find vulnerabilities and patch them much faster. In biology, you’d want better detection, better diagnostics, and the ability to develop countermeasures quickly.

But I don’t think you can just say, “Well, we’ll have good AI fighting bad AI, and everything will work out.” You have to ask whether the structure of the problem favors defense. Does the defender have to succeed every time, while the attacker only has to succeed once? Are there bottlenecks where a relatively small investment could make an entire system more resilient? Those details matter enormously.

And then there’s the deployment problem. Having a powerful defensive technology in a lab isn’t the same as having it operating in hospitals, in government, or across critical infrastructure. You need institutions that can evaluate these tools, adopt them, and respond quickly when something changes. So I’d want us investing in the technical defenses, but also practicing how we actually use them. The time to build that capacity is before the threat becomes acute.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses building technical defenses and institutions, but does not suggest consulting AIs about how to design societal structures.

r002.rationale: It says AI is advancing rapidly, but does not distinguish how far capabilities may exceed today's from how soon they may arrive.

r003.rationale: The candidate notes challenges in defense and deployment, but does not attribute difficulty anticipating societal defenses to future capabilities being far beyond current ones.
